Abstract:

Starting in the 1910s, Bengal witnessed an alternative printing culture of little magazines. Its experiments included, but were not limited to, providing literary space to young writers which nurtured new voices, experimenting with language and style, and exploring the tabooed space. The little magazines gradually evolved and functioned as a counter site of experiments, discontinuities, and resistance, thereby paving ways of challenging the predominant print culture of contemporary Bengal. Moreover, these advance guard literary platforms promoted marginal voices&mdashparticularly refugees, Dalits, and women&mdashto articulate their resistance towards dominant cultural values and ideologies. This study examines the contribution of Bangla little magazines published since the 1910s in reshaping modern literary culture through formal, linguistic, and thematic transgressions, thereby contesting canon formation and institutional authority in Bengal. It traces their emergence as transgressive platforms through which marginalized voices articulated dissent, and significantly challenged the disciplinary history and mainstream literary practices. In addition, this study explores their contemporary transformations in response to globalization, digital publishing, and social media, underscoring their continued relevance as dynamic sites of cultural resistance.
